Leeks
lēks
n. pl. (a plant of the onion kind; third in Israel's list of Egyptian food)
Old English leac, a plant of the onion family — the same element in garlick and in hemlock. The Hebrew chatsir ordinarily means grass or green herbage, and is rendered leeks only here.

Biblical Definition

The word belongs to the same verse as the melons and the garlick: “We remember the fish, which we did eat in Egypt freely; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlick” (Num 11:5). The Hebrew behind it is worth noticing, because chatsir is the word used for the grass that withereth and for the green thing that springs up — the commonest, cheapest growth there is. Israel is grieving over greens. That is exactly the force the passage wants: the things they wept for were not delicacies but the ordinary fare of a labouring people, and they still weighed more in the moment than manna and a promised land. Moses' own words in the chapter show what the complaint cost the man who had to carry it — he asks whether he begat this people, and whether he is to carry them in his bosom as a nursing father. The leeks of Egypt broke a prophet before they were done.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines the leek as a plant of the genus Allium, cultivated for its bulb and leaves, allied to the onion and garlic.

expand to see more

LEEK, n. [Sax. leac.] A plant of the genus Allium, having a bulbous root and long green leaves.

It is cultivated for kitchen use, and is allied to the onion.

The leeks, and the onions, and the garlick. Num. xi.

LEEK-GREEN, a. Of a green color resembling that of a leek.

Key Scripture

Num 11:5 — "We remember the fish, which we did eat in Egypt freely; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlick:"

Num 11:6 — "But now our soul is dried away: there is nothing at all, beside this manna, before our eyes."

Exo 16:3 — "And the children of Israel said unto them, Would to God we had died by the hand of the LORD in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the flesh pots, and when we did eat bread to the full; for ye have brought us forth into this wilderness, to kill this whole assembly with hunger."

Pro 15:16 — "Better is little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure and trouble therewith."

Modern Corruption

Complaint is now spoken of as honesty and even as courage, while Scripture calls the murmuring of Numbers 11 what it was and records what it cost.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the distinction between lament and murmuring, which Scripture draws sharply and our vocabulary has lost. Lament is addressed to God, argues with Him on the basis of His own promises, and is all through the Psalms; a third of the Psalter is complaint, and God put it in the songbook. Murmuring is spoken about God to one another, it re-narrates the past to indict Him, and it spreads. Numbers 11 is murmuring: the people wept in the doors of their tents, every man in the door of his tent, and the complaint moved outward through the camp until Moses himself was undone by it. The test is not whether a man is sad or even angry — Job was both — but whether he is taking it to God or circulating it.

The second thing worth marking is what murmuring does to leadership. Moses' response in this chapter is one of the frankest speeches in the Old Testament: he tells God the burden is too heavy, that he did not conceive this people, and that if this is how it is to be he would rather be killed out of hand. God does not rebuke him. He appoints seventy elders and puts of the spirit upon them, dividing the load. That is providence answering exhaustion with help rather than with a reprimand, and it is worth remembering by anyone carrying a congregation, a household, or a company of murmurers. The leeks were the smallest thing imaginable to break a man over. They still nearly did.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chatsir (H2682), grass, green herbage — rendered leeks only at Numbers 11:5; with luwn (H3885), to murmur or lodge overnight in complaint.

expand to see more

Hebrew chatsir (H2682) — grass, green growth; rendered leeks in the list, and grass in the psalms; Numbers 11:5, Psalm 103:15.

Hebrew luwn (H3885) — to lodge, and hence to murmur; the standing verb for Israel's complaining; Exodus 16:2.

Hebrew bakah (H1058) — to weep; they wept, every man in the door of his tent; Numbers 11:10.

Hebrew massa (H4853) — a burden; Moses asks why God laid the burden of this people on him; Numbers 11:11.

Greek gogguzo (G1111) — to murmur; neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured; 1 Corinthians 10:10.

Usage

"“The leeks, and the onions” — the cheapest greens there were."

"“Our soul is dried away” — said by men eating bread from heaven."

"“Better is little with the fear of the LORD” — the proverb the camp had forgotten."
